Convert a number written as digits in one base into its digits in another.

Adapted from Exercism's [problem specification](https://github.com/exercism/problem-specifications/tree/main/exercises/all-your-base) (MIT). Listed under [Numbers & Math](/examples/?subject=numbers-and-math).

```nomi-run
// FILE: all_your_base.nomi
/// Why a number cannot be rebased.
pub enum Error {
    InvalidInputBase
    InvalidDigit
    InvalidOutputBase
}

/// The digits, most significant first, of the number that `digits` writes
/// in `input_base`, written in `output_base`. Zero, and an empty list of
/// digits, come out as `[0]`.
pub fn rebase(input_base: Int, digits: List<Int>, output_base: Int) -> Result<List<Int>, Error> {
    if input_base < 2 {
        return Err(.InvalidInputBase)
    }

    if Iter.any?(digits, fn d -> d < 0 or d >= input_base) {
        return Err(.InvalidDigit)
    }

    if output_base < 2 {
        return Err(.InvalidOutputBase)
    }

    number = Iter.reduce(digits, fn total = 0, d -> total * input_base + d)
    Ok(digits_of(number, output_base))
}

fn digits_of(number: Int, base: Int) -> List<Int> {
    if number == 0 { return [0] }

    Iter.iterate(number, &(&1 / base))
    |> Iter.take_while(&(&1 > 0))
    |> Iter.map(&(&1 % base))
    |> Iter.reverse()
}

// FILE: all_your_base_test.nomi
import {
    all_your_base
    all_your_base.Error
}

test "rebases digits" {
    cases = [
        #("single bit one to decimal", 2, [1], 10, Ok([1])),
        #("binary to single decimal", 2, [1, 0, 1], 10, Ok([5])),
        #("single decimal to binary", 10, [5], 2, Ok([1, 0, 1])),
        #("binary to multiple decimal", 2, [1, 0, 1, 0, 1, 0], 10, Ok([4, 2])),
        #("decimal to binary", 10, [4, 2], 2, Ok([1, 0, 1, 0, 1, 0])),
        #("trinary to hexadecimal", 3, [1, 1, 2, 0], 16, Ok([2, 10])),
        #("hexadecimal to trinary", 16, [2, 10], 3, Ok([1, 1, 2, 0])),
        #("15-bit integer", 97, [3, 46, 60], 73, Ok([6, 10, 45])),
        #("empty list", 2, [], 10, Ok([0])),
        #("single zero", 10, [0], 2, Ok([0])),
        #("multiple zeros", 10, [0, 0, 0], 2, Ok([0])),
        #("leading zeros", 7, [0, 6, 0], 10, Ok([4, 2])),
        #("input base is one", 1, [0], 10, Err(Error.InvalidInputBase)),
        #("input base is zero", 0, [], 10, Err(.InvalidInputBase)),
        #("input base is negative", -2, [1], 10, Err(.InvalidInputBase)),
        #("negative digit", 2, [1, -1, 1, 0, 1, 0], 10, Err(.InvalidDigit)),
        #("invalid positive digit", 2, [1, 2, 1, 0, 1, 0], 10, Err(.InvalidDigit)),
        #("output base is one", 2, [1, 0, 1, 0, 1, 0], 1, Err(.InvalidOutputBase)),
        #("output base is zero", 10, [7], 0, Err(.InvalidOutputBase)),
        #("output base is negative", 2, [1], -7, Err(.InvalidOutputBase)),
        #("both bases are negative", -2, [1], -7, Err(.InvalidInputBase)),
    ]

    subtests cases, #(description, input_base, digits, output_base, expected), description {
        assert all_your_base.rebase(input_base, digits, output_base) == expected
    }
}
```

## How it's written

- Errors are an `Error` enum with one variant per canonical message. The checks run in the canonical order (input base, digits, output base), so "both bases are negative" reports the input base.
- Each check is an early `return`, which keeps the conversion unindented.
- The digits become a number with `Iter.reduce` (`total * input_base + d`), and the number becomes digits with `Iter.iterate` divided down to zero, each step taken `% base`, then `Iter.reverse`. Zero and an empty list both come out `[0]` through one early return.
- The 21 cases are one `subtests` table. The first error row writes `Err(Error.InvalidInputBase)` and the later ones `Err(.InvalidDigit)`: a qualified variant in an earlier row gives the enum to the bare ones after it, so the table needs no type annotation.
